title: US Senate Advances Bill Threatening 100% Tariffs on India, China Over Russian Oil
excerpt: The bipartisan legislation, named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, passed a key vote 86-12 and would authorize sweeping sanctions on Russia alongside tariff authority targeting major buyers of Russian energy.
body:
• The US Senate advanced a bipartisan bill 86-12 that would allow 100% tariffs on goods from the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas, including India and China
  • Named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, the bill also imposes new sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, and the shadow fleet used to evade oil export restrictions
  • The legislation must still pass the House, which is on summer recess and unlikely to act before September

The US Senate has advanced a bipartisan bill that could expose India and China to tariffs of up to 100% on their exports to the United States, as part of a broader effort to punish countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas.

The measure, named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026, passed a key procedural vote 86-12 on July 30, with support from nearly all Republicans and a majority of Democrats.

What the Bill Does

The legislation authorizes the US president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the world’s top five buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. According to Senate aides, the current top five crude purchasers are China, India, Slovakia, Hungary, and Azerbaijan.

The bill includes an exemption for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s total natural gas exports and are taking significant steps to reduce those imports — a provision that would shield Japan, France, Hungary, and Belgium. The US Trade Representative would reassess the top five purchasers every 180 days and adjust tariff rates accordingly.

Beyond tariffs, the legislation imposes mandatory sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions, and vessels in the so-called “shadow fleet” that Moscow uses to bypass oil export restrictions. At President Trump’s request, the revised bill also extends sanctions targeting Iran’s energy and weapons sectors.

A Tribute to Lindsey Graham

The bill is named after the late Republican Senator from South Carolina, who died suddenly in mid-July after spending more than a year building bipartisan support for the legislation. Graham had reached an agreement with President Trump to move forward with the bill just a day before his death, during a trip to Ukraine.

“There is no greater way to honor Senator Graham’s legacy than to move forward with this bipartisan agreement.”

— Joint statement from six Republican and Democratic senators

Graham’s sister Darline, appointed to complete his Senate term, said she looked forward to passing the legislation and sending it to the president’s desk.

Concerns Over Presidential Power

Despite broad bipartisan support, some Democrats have raised concerns. Senator Ron Wyden and Representative Richard Neal warned the tariffs could raise import costs for American consumers and potentially hurt European allies.

A document prepared by the Democratic staff on the Senate Finance Committee noted that “additional countries can continually be brought into scope, and vague scoping criteria give Trump far too much opportunity to abuse these powers.” The bill contains no mechanism for congressional disapproval of tariffs, and the presidential authority never expires.

Representative Gregory Meeks praised the sanctions on Russia’s shadow fleet but called the tariff provisions “a massive backdoor authority for President Trump to impose more tariffs.”

Impact on India

India has been one of the largest buyers of discounted Russian crude since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The country’s energy imports from Russia have drawn repeated scrutiny from Western allies, though India has maintained that its purchases serve its energy security needs.

If enacted, the bill would mark the first time Congress has explicitly authorized tariffs as a geopolitical tool to punish countries financing another nation’s war effort. Analysts at Rapidan Energy Group expect Trump could use the tariff threat as a bargaining chip in broader trade negotiations with India.

What Happens Next

The legislation must still pass the House of Representatives, which left Washington for its summer recess and is unlikely to take up the bill before September. An earlier version of the legislation proposed tariffs of 500% on Russian energy buyers — the revised 100% cap was designed to build broader support.

The bill also exempts purchases of Russian uranium by the US for nuclear reactors and medical isotopes, and excludes activities under US-Russia cooperation in nuclear and space sectors.
